summary: Wilhelm Dilger (1855–1920) was a scholar in linguistics and Indology. He served as a missionary with the Basel Mission from 1880 to 1907 and held a post at the University of Tübingen in 1910.

Wilhelm Dilthey (1833–1911) was a philosopher who studied at Heidelberg University and Humboldt University of Berlin. He held posts at the universities of Basel (~1866–1868), Kiel (~1868–1871), Breslau (~1871–1882), and Berlin (~1882–1911).

Wilhelm Eggers (b. 1888) worked in Indology. He studied at the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, the German Colonial School, and Kiel University, earning a Ph.D. between 1924 and 1929 under Friedrich Otto Schrader (~1921–1927).
Wilhelm Ferdinand Hüttemann (b. 1871) worked in Indology. He completed his Ph.D. in 1890 at the University of Strasbourg, where he studied under Ernst Leumann.

Wilhelm Filchner (1877–1957) worked in Tibetology, history and archaeology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at the Prussian Military Academy, Humboldt University of Berlin, Königsberg, and Munich, later becoming a professor at Berlin in 1938.

Wilhelm Gampert (1902–1987) worked in Indology, studying at the German University in Prague (~1923–1928, Ph.D.) under Moriz Winternitz and Otto Stein. From 1945 to 1978, he was a scientific worker at the Czech Academy of Sciences.

Wilhelm Geiger (1856–1943) worked in Indology, linguistics, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He earned his Ph.D. under Friedrich von Spiegel at Erlangen-Nuremberg, where he became professor in 1891, before serving as professor at Munich (1920–1924).

Wilhelm Germann (1840–1902) specialized in Indology, religious studies, and history and archaeology. He studied at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg (~1859–1863) and held a post at the Leipzig Evangelical Lutheran Mission in 1864.

Wilhelm Gesenius (1786–1842) was a scholar of linguistics and religious studies. After studying at Helmstedt and Göttingen under Thomas Christian Tychsen, he held posts at the University of Göttingen (~1806–1809) and Halle-Wittenberg (~1810–1842).

Wilhelm Grube (1855–1908) was a sinologist and linguist who studied at Saint Petersburg and Leipzig. He served at the Asiatic Museum, Berlin's Ethnological Museum, and taught at Humboldt University of Berlin, becoming extraordinary professor in 1892.
Wilhelm Gundert (1880–1971) was a scholar in Japanology and religious studies. He succeeded Karl Florenz and held a post at the University of Hamburg from approximately 1936 to 1945.

Wilhelm Halbfass (1940–2000) was an Indologist and philosopher educated at Vienna, Göttingen (Ph.D. under Ernst Waldschmidt), and Hamburg. He held faculty posts at Brock University and later at the University of Pennsylvania (1973–1974, 1982–2000).

Wilhelm Havers (1879–1961) was a linguist and Indologist who studied at Tübingen, Leipzig, and Berlin. He was a professor at Bern (1915), Würzburg (1920), Breslau (1929), and the University of Vienna (1937–1953).

Wilhelm Jahn (b. 1873) worked in Indology, studying at Berlin, Marburg, Rostock, Kiel, Leipzig, and Würzburg (Ph.D., 1902–1903). He taught at the University of Zurich (1909–1918) and Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg (1918–1919).

Wilhelm K. Essler (b. 1940) specializes in philosophy and Indology. He studied at the University of Munich (~1960–1966) under Wolfgang Stegmüller and Wilhelm Britzelmayr, and served as Director of the Institute for Philosophy at Goethe University Frankfurt (~1986–2005).

Wilhelm Koppers (1886–1961) worked in Indology, religious studies, and history/archaeology. He studied at Missionshaus St. Gabriel and the University of Vienna (Ph.D. 1914–1917), where he later served as PD (1924–1938) and professor/director (1945–1957).

Wilhelm Krause (1910–1976) was a scholar in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian/Central Asian studies. Educated at the University of Vienna and the University of Graz, he served at Graz as Lektor for Sanskrit (1960) and eo. Professor (1968).

Wilhelm Max Müller (1862–1919) was a scholar in history, archaeology, and linguistics. He studied at Humboldt University of Berlin and the University of Leipzig, and later held a post at the University of Pennsylvania (~1906–1919).

Wilhelm Pertsch (1832–1899) was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Berlin under Franz Bopp and at Tübingen under Rudolf von Roth. He spent his career in Gotha as head librarian and director at Schloss Friedenstein.

Wilhelm Printz (1887–1941) worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at Leipzig, Göttingen, Berlin (Ph.D. under Heinrich Lüders), and Frankfurt. He served as librarian for the Deutsche Morgenländische Gesellschaft and professor at Halle-Wittenberg (1929–1939).
